#8263. Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.)

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#8262. Buried By a Sudden Snowstorm in the Himalayas, 29 Hikers Faced a Fight to Survive

The trek over Auden’s Col in India’s Garhwal Himalayas is no stroll: Crossing the pass means working hard at elevations of up to 18,000 feet, crossing a glacier, and, occasionally, dealing with some of the world’s worst weather.

It was that last hazard that an expedition faced earlier this fall, when a freak snowstorm dropped more than six feet of powder on them with little notice. The 29-member team from Indian outfitter Aquaterra Adventures had reached base camp at 16,400 feet when the weather took a turn for the worse, battering them with heavy snowfall, temperatures down to -4 Fahrenheit, and 62-mile-per-hour winds.

While Jetendra Singh Rana, their lead guide, quickly called off their ascent and sent a message asking for rescue, the storm had flattened many of the group’s tents, leaving them all to squeeze into one remaining cook tent while they waited for help to come. Backpacker contributor Karthika Gupta spoke to expedition members to hear their story; read her full article and see footage from the  group’s ordeal here. –Adam Roy, Editor-in-Chief

#8261. Hannah Otto Broke Her Leg Descending Kilimanjaro—and Kept Riding

Hannah Otto celebrates at Uhuru Peak, the 19,341-foot summit of Mount Kilimanjaro in Tanzania, with her mountain bike. (Photo: Rachael Galipo)

By the time professional mountain biker Hannah Otto, 30, reached the final miles of her descent from Mount Kilimanjaro, 19,341 feet, she had already navigated the mountain’s most punishing terrain. She’d hauled her bike up snowy slopes, scrambled over boulders at 18,000 feet, and ridden steep, rocky trails where softball-sized stones shifted beneath her tires. Now she was on a rainforest dirt road easy enough to ride on a gravel bike.

On November 3, Otto became the first known woman to ascend and descend Africa’s tallest mountain with a bicycle in a single day. She completed the effort in 10 hours, 18 minutes, and 51 seconds, despite breaking her leg just two miles from the finish.

“I came around a gentle bend in the trail, and the trail went from dry dirt to mud, and it was like I hit ice,” Otto told Outside. “The bike just came out from underneath me, and I was on the ground in a second.”

The fall had broken her leg. But two miles from the finish, she got back on her bike and rode out.

The attempt was also part of a fundraising campaign for World Bicycle Relief, a nonprofit that provides bicycles to improve access to education, healthcare, and employment. Otto hopes to raise $165,000 to provide 1,000 bicycles to rural African communities.

Otto’s ride established the first known women’s time for a single-day bicycle ascent and descent of Kilimanjaro. Canadian mountain biker Cory Wallace completed an ascent and descent in 8 hours, 55 minutes in 2022, but no verified women’s time had been recorded before Otto’s attempt.

Otto, who has raced mountain bikes for 21 years, spent months preparing for the altitude and dramatic changes in terrain. Kilimanjaro rises through rainforest, heath and moorland, and alpine desert before reaching its snow-covered summit. Otto said temperatures ranged from about 70 degrees Fahrenheit near the base to 10 degrees near the top.

She trained as often as possible above 10,000 feet in Utah’s mountains, scheduled races at higher elevations, and added heat and sauna sessions to her routine. She also hiked on a steep treadmill with a sandbag on her back to train for carrying her bike.

After seven days acclimatizing on Kilimanjaro, Otto returned to the base, rested a day, and started her single-day attempt at 3 a.m. with a support team that included her husband, a film crew, and local Tanzanian guides, aiming to beat the afternoon storm

At about 15,500 feet, the terrain became too steep to pedal. Otto strapped her bike to her back and spent three and a half hours hiking three miles up snow-covered slopes approaching a 40 percent grade. Near 18,000 feet, she scrambled over large boulders with her hands, the bike still strapped to her back.

“With every 1,000 feet up the mountain, it felt like the bike gained five pounds,” she said.

Otto had planned three different ways to carry the bike, rotating between them for relief. Meanwhile, the altitude shortened her steps, raised her heart rate, and made every stumble harder to recover from.

Snow began falling just as she reached the summit. After hiking down the first steep section, she got back on her bike, thinking she’d beaten the worst of the weather. But rain had soaked the rainforest trails below.

After the crash, Otto tried twice to stand.

“I watched my leg go in two completely different directions, and it was the most painful thing I’ve ever felt in my life,” Otto told Outside. “Both times, I fell to the ground screaming.”

Her nearest guide was about 15 minutes behind her and could radio for a one-wheeled stretcher to carry her out. At first, she waited for help.

But as she lay there, supine on the muddy floor of the Tanzanian rainforest, Otto told Outside that she imagined herself at 60, explaining that she’d been physically capable of finishing but had fallen short because of an accident. At the time, the thought made her sick. Living with that disappointment, she decided, would hurt worse than whatever her injured leg might put her through on the way down.

She army-crawled through the mud to retrieve her bike, used it as a crutch to stand, lowered the dropper seatpost, and draped her chest over the saddle to shimmy into a seated position.

Most of the remaining trail was downhill, allowing her to coast. Still, every bump sent pain through her broken leg. She used one hand to lift the injured leg onto the pedal for support, then moved it out of the way to pedal uphill with her good leg.

“There was also a piece of me that was riding out of fear and survival, even though it was excruciating,” Otto said.

When Otto finally reached the finish, about 20 Tanzanian team members sang, danced, and clapped as she approached. They knew she’d summited, but nobody had told them about the crash. As soon as they saw her condition, the celebration stopped.

Within minutes, the team had loaded her into a vehicle for the 45-minute drive over rough roads to the nearest hospital, where X-rays confirmed the break.

Rather than undergo surgery in Tanzania, Otto made the roughly 30-hour journey home with her broken leg. Back in Salt Lake City, she underwent surgery for two tibial plateau fractures and an associated ACL injury. She expects eight to ten weeks without putting weight on her leg, but hopes to return to racing in April 2027.

Despite the injury, Otto said the experience has changed how she thinks about her own abilities.

“Now I feel like I have this story and this moment that I can always lean back on and be like, ‘You are so tough, Hannah,'” she said. “For me, that is the most reassuring thing that I could gift myself.”

#8260. The Glacier Died—And the Trail Runners Started Coming

I’m standing with Samuel Mendoza on top of Chacaltaya Mountain, 17,785 feet above sea level. Under our feet is a sharp slope of scree, a jumbled descent of rocks with patches of snow. The air is thin, and the vast Bolivian landscape surrounds us.

Directly ahead, the Altiplano—the high plain—stretches from the foot of the mountain. El Alto, the chaotic concrete and red brick city that has grown to roughly 900,000 people, lies at the far edge of the plain at 13,000 feet of elevation, crammed against a canyon’s edge. About 1,500 feet below and connected by a series of cable cars, La Paz, Bolivia’s seat of government, sprawls.

Behind us rises the Huayna Potosí massif. The nearly 20,000-foot summit towers above, its glaciated peak passing in and out of fast-moving clouds. About 45 miles to the northwest, Lake Titicaca—the central motif to Inca creation stories—shimmers on the horizon.

It’s here, on this high mountain of almost-bare rock cradled in the Andes, that Mendoza learned to ski.

Located roughly 20 miles north of La Paz, Chacaltaya was once the world’s highest-altitude ski resort. It began in the 1930s when Raúl Posnansky, an engineer and ski enthusiast, recognized the mountain’s potential, according to 2023 reporting by “Radio Ambulante.” Chacaltaya’s glacier, though relatively small in area at roughly 55 acres, was a solid tongue of ice descending the slope. Temperatures up high stayed low, and snow fell heavily and often during the wet season. The ice was there, had always been there, and would always be there, by all indications at the time.

Posnansky worked to materialize his skiing fantasy: He hired laborers to build an access road, haul materials, construct cabins, and install the first rope tow at Chacaltaya—powered by a truck engine housed in a cabin hanging over the base of the ski run.

Posnansky, along with other mountain athletes, founded the Club Andino Boliviano, a group of dedicated skiers and enthusiasts. To fund the growing ski scene, the club drew involvement from La Paz’s middle and upper classes, and Posnansky and the club persuaded Bolivia’s Congress to pass tax legislation dedicating 1% of the country’s hotel revenue to Bolivia’s Ski and Mountaineering Federation. This funding would help transform Chacaltaya from a passion project into the hub of Bolivian skiing—a hub that, while retaining its roughshod, backyard roots, would grow to host a national ski team, crowded weekend races, the first South American ski championships, and athletes who would represent the country at Winter Olympics.

When Mendoza was a young boy in El Alto, his family wasn’t connected to La Paz’s urban elite who would drive across the Altiplano to ski. Mendoza’s father, however, worked as the caretaker of Chacaltaya, often living for weeks at a time at the resort to maintain the facilities.

When he was 15, Mendoza accompanied his father to the mountain for the first time. He spent his first night at the base racked by altitude sickness.

“My dad gave me coca leaf tea,” he says. The next day, “the sun came out; I felt better. I got acclimated, and I learned to ski.”

Fifty years later, standing once again on the summit, Mendoza is transported back to the resort’s heyday.

“The rope would drop us off here,” he says. “And then …” He puts his hands on bent knees and waves them back and forth in a slalom. He raises his hands over his head and lets out a high yell, feeling the old rush of racing in the cold air.

Mendoza is in his 60s now. He has a harder time seeing, looking out through thick glasses, and his knees sometimes bother him.

Around us the glacier has completely vanished, leaving behind only a mountain of rock.

Infatuated with the world of snow and slopes, Mendoza learned to ski on gear borrowed from Club Andino. He worked long, physical days with his father, tasks ranging from construction and upkeep to manning the rope tow—including rebraiding the wire cable whenever it snapped, a job that left Mendoza with thin white scars across his fingers. From his father, he learned to manage the mountain, the two often sleeping in the lodge for weeks at a time.

Meanwhile, his love for skiing only deepened. Mendoza remembers Stanley Shepard, an American diplomat posted in Bolivia, who taught him advanced techniques and shared the joy of the mountain.

“Stan would drive up this road so fast,” he says as we drive the same route from the city to Chacaltaya some 50 years later. He smiles with the memory of the adrenaline rush.

Mendoza’s ski story exists in a split reality: In one, he is the caretaker’s son, surrounded by a country’s elites who lived near, but not next to, families like his. The socioeconomic divide paralleled the geography: La Paz’s wealthy neighborhoods in the valley, El Alto on the cold outcropping of the Altiplano above. Despite the divide, Mendoza was a vital member of the Chacaltaya scene; the members of Club Andino were his friends. The nights were full of music whenever others would sleep alongside him and his father at the refugio. The period is marked in Mendoza’s mind by shared meals in the cabin and shared runs on the mountain.

By the 1970s, with Chacaltaya entering its golden period, Mendoza was both employee and skier. He tells me he used to set up for the weekend slalom races—ones he’d often compete in as well. I ask about the slalom poles, curious about infrastructure. He tells me they were made nearby. “But the first times,” he says, “we used hollow canes, like cornstalks.”

In a 1976 article in Ski Magazine, American writer Jeff Frees described his visit to the ski hill. There were some two dozen weekly skiers sharing the piste and “a slightly doglegged swath of snow” that was “lined with rocks from top to bottom,” although there were no lift lines, he writes.

The chalet, perched on a rocky precipice, was “so frightening and insecure-looking,” that “some skiers refused to enter it,” Frees says. With the altitude nearing 18,000 feet, other visitors didn’t even bother trying, exiting the minibus up from La Paz only to climb into the truck heading back down the road.

This was the electric, eclectic golden period. One 1,000-foot run served by a single rope tow prone to snapping and powered by a truck engine. A handful of foreign visitors and the dedicated group of Club Andino members. A small, warm refugio built on a cliffside, filled with coca tea, quinoa soup, and music. Weekend races and training events for young locals, supporting ski teams who would go on to participate in four consecutive Olympics starting in 1980. And behind this incredible scene was Samuel Mendoza.

“It was frozen all the time,” Mendoza says. “The people said, ‘This is forever. It will never recede.’”

“But little by little, it started to thaw.”

Scientists had been documenting Chacaltaya for decades, but a systematic study of the glacier began in 1991, led in part by Edson Ramírez of the Universidad Mayor de San Andrés in La Paz (UMSA). Glaciologists’ observations began to echo the concerns skiers had voiced for years: Chacaltaya was melting—and fast.

“Snow would fall at night,” Mendoza says, “but it would be gone by midday.” As temperatures rose, the glacier retreated, exposing more and more of the rock underneath.

While the retreat was evident in some of the earliest photos from the 1940s, Ramírez and his team found that, in just six years from 1992 to 1998, the glacier’s melt had accelerated dramatically, losing more than 40% of its surface area and roughly two-thirds of its ice volume. The team’s prediction: The glacier would disappear within 10 to 15 years.

By 2009, the glacier was completely gone.

“The entire glacier of the world’s highest ski slope had turned to water,” Mendoza reflects.

As the ski run melted under them, various last-ditch efforts were implemented to keep the sport alive. Artificial snow production was attempted, but ultimately proved too costly. Moving the resort to other nearby mountains was considered, but transportation and access were constant hurdles. Even traditional Andean rituals were offered to the mountain gods.

But the glacier, once gone, would not come back.

Without their ski hub, the Club Andino eventually unraveled. A photo hangs in the abandoned refugio of smiling members piled outside the club. Mendoza tells me their names—a running list of friends moved abroad or passed away. Even their headquarters in La Paz is now shuttered.

While sooner than expected, Chacaltaya’s glacier death was not unique within the broader scope of Andean glaciers. Research published in 2026 by Giuliana Adrianzen and Andrew Malone of the University of Illinois Chicago found that Bolivia’s Cordillera Real lost a stunning 42% of its glaciated area between 1992 and 2024.

This trend is widespread across the Andes, which are home to 99% of the world’s tropical glacier area—particularly vulnerable ice fields located near the Earth’s equator.

Glaciers in this latitudinal band are much more susceptible to small temperature changes than those outside of it. Kept frozen primarily by extreme altitude, tropical glaciers already exist close to the temperature threshold to sustain permanent ice; they also don’t experience the long, cold winters of glaciers nearer the poles. Andean glaciers are now thinning 35% faster than the global average, according to a 2025 international report co-authored by researchers at the University of Sheffield. As global warming pushes the freezing level higher, more precipitation falls on these glaciers as rain instead of snow, accelerating the melt.

Over the 60 years between 1960 and 2020, Peru lost 56% of its glacier area. In 2024, Venezuela was declared glacier-free with the death of the Humboldt Glacier (named, perhaps ominously, after the German naturalist who pioneered the notion that everything in the natural world is connected). Colombia is following the same trajectory, having lost more than 90% of its glaciated area since the mid-1800s.

According to UNESCO, the Andes could lose 78 to 97% of their tropical glacier volume by the year 2100.

Of course, more than skiing is at risk—including the water supply risk of some 90 million people across the Andes. These glaciers serve as water reserves for the millions of people who live downstream, and their disappearance foreshadows looming ecological disasters. Many Andean municipalities also rely on hydroelectric power, which depends on steady dry-season meltwater from the glaciers. As the glaciers shrink, that flow is dwindling, increasing the severity of droughts.

While Chacaltaya’s lift has long since stopped spinning, a handful of trained guides and foreign clients continue to practice ski mountaineering in Bolivia, climbing high peaks and bombing descents on still-intact glaciers. While the chalet has ceased to function, the mountain remains an active scientific base. The Chacaltaya Observatory, run by UMSA’s Laboratory for Atmospheric Physics—with multiple international collaborators—continues to measure the atmosphere, climate, and cosmic rays.

And although skiing has abandoned the mountain, Mendoza has not.

Since his father died on Chacaltaya over 30 years ago, Mendoza has served as the mountain’s main caretaker, a position he continues to hold. He spends more time in El Alto with his family now, but he and his brother Adolfo still make multiple trips a week to Chacaltaya, welcoming the handful of tourists who come to visit the abandoned chalet or use it as an acclimatization hike. With the small collected entrance fees, he pays for repairs and maintains his memories of the resort.

Many of Mendoza’s days, however, are spent in solitude, standing alone at 17,000 feet on Chacaltaya’s rocky remains.

“When you’re alone it’s a little sad,” he says. “With only the birds, the condors, the Andean foxes.”

Since the collapse of the glacier, a new group of athletes has taken to Chacaltaya: trail runners—whose arrival is directly tied to skiing’s disappearance. Paolo Choque is the director of skyrunning for the Bolivian Ski and Mountaineering Federation. One of the “last people to learn to ski in Bolivia,” Choque witnessed the collapse of skiing at Chacaltaya, and he has since helped cultivate trail running to take its place.

In 2001, when Choque learned to ski, the main chunk of the glacier was already “ruined,” he says. Against the backdrop of the dying mountain, Choque became involved in promoting skiing and snowboarding in Bolivia, including searching for alternative mountains to host competitions.

In 2011, the federation found another suitable slope at nearby Charquini and hosted a Bolivian Ski Championship. Choque says that snowboarding grew in popularity over a handful of years with the promotion efforts, but participation numbers remained low—with just 25 racers in the snowboard event in 2015. Amid melting ice and low participation, he made the decision to pivot. “I said, ‘No, this isn’t going anywhere. We don’t even have a ski slope.’”

Inspired by the sport’s explosion in Spain, Choque organized a pilot skyrunning race on Chacaltaya in 2016, which was met with a strong reception. Athletes had returned to the mountain. The federation’s championship now draws about 200 participants each year, according to Choque. Racers gain points at multiple events across the country, which take place over otherworldly terrain—from the world’s largest salt flats in Uyuni to the folds of the Sajama stratovolcano, the shores of Lake Titicaca, and, of course, Chacaltaya Mountain.

“Skiing may have died,” Choque says, “but mountain sports have not.”

While private trail races have also increased in popularity in Bolivia over the past decade, the federation aims to develop skyrunning and its next generation of athletes through accessible competition. Race entries, Choque emphasizes, are kept inexpensive, and youth competition categories give athletes the opportunity to qualify for international competition.

“For me, sport must come first, and it must be accessible to everyone,” Choque says.

Despite challenges with funding, Choque says the federation has seen success in sending participants to compete in the South American Championships, where they have earned podium finishes, including three medals in 2025.

As one sport fades and another grows, Choque defines what success could look like for Bolivian skyrunning.

“What I want to achieve is to bring a South American championship here, and if possible, even a youth world championship to Bolivia,” he says. “We have the potential.”

Paolo and the federation hope that Chacaltaya will continue to be an important mountain hub for decades to come—with or without the glacier.

For all of the uniqueness of Chacaltaya’s history, it does mirror a larger global skiing trend: most of the participants were wealthy. Mendoza remembers well the divide caused by the cost of equipment. “From the city of El Alto there weren’t a lot of skiers,” he says.

Through the Ski and Mountaineering Federation, Choque is determined that the next iteration of Chacaltaya’s mountain sports—trail and sky running—do not follow the same pattern. Mendoza, meanwhile, has seen some of the runners who are taking to the mountain to train where he once skied. I ask him if he would ever run one of the races, and he tells me he enjoys running. His knees, though, keep him from doing too much of it. But when a German tourist wanted to race from the summit to the lagoon below, Mendoza happily said yes.

“Replacing skiing at Chacaltaya in the future is possible,” he says.

Looking across the dry slope where he learned to ski, the rusted remains of his rope tow, the faded chalet and the memories contained, Mendoza takes a deep breath. At the end of the day, as we drive the winding dirt road down to the city with Chacaltaya shrinking into the distance behind us, he looks ahead.

“It makes me happy when people visit the mountain,” he says.

#8259. On Climbing Mount Robson’s Emperor Face Alone

High on the Emperor Ridge of Mount Robson, enjoying lunch in the sun. (Photo: Anton Korsun)

There is a cinema up north. Beyond the rising northern star, beyond the Icefields Parkway, and far beyond the chaos and clamor of the Banff Mountain Film Festival—it is built in the image of a gothic cathedral and shrouded in storm. This cinema operates year round. It has no dress code, schedule, or rules on serving alcohol to minors. Inside, every visitor watches their own film: Some see triumph and elation. Others see despair, retreat, or a kaleidoscope of rock and ice before the front doors shut forever and the silver screen goes deathly black. Yet others simply stand alone in its great white hall, listening to the sound of silence and watching mountain ranges stretch to the horizon like limbs of a great white spider.

This is a film review of sorts. In September of 2026 I soloed Infinite Patience on the Emperor Face of Mount Robson. I’ve been asked to write about it. I’ve been asked why I haven’t posted anything on social media or pontificated my radness to the press. Frankly, it’s because I am a rather poor film critic.

There is no doubt in my mind that alpine climbing is more art than sport.

If I were to ask you—how did Usain Bolt run 100 meters in 9.58 seconds?

“Well, he moved his legs quite fast,” you might say.

But can you tell me how Voytek Kurtyka and Robert Schauer suffered up the Shining Wall of Gasherbrum IV (7,925m) in a 10-day sleep-and-food-deprived push? Or how Steve House and Marko Prezelj clawed their way to the summit of the North Twin with one missing boot and two coreshot ropes? Because I can’t.

I sit in awe of the performers on stage as they pull another rabbit from their hats or escape the icy chains of some far-flung north face yet again. The beauty of alpinism is similar to the beauty of theater, dance, and stage magic—an illusion of wizardry brought about by true mastery of the performers.

However, while similar, alpinism and theater are not the same. Climbing has no audience and no stage. Climbing media has both. In recent times it has become too easy to convince ourselves that perception equals participation—that by clicking that “follow” button or watching that film we can stand in the shoes of the artist. But we can’t. Because to believe otherwise would be to mistake climbing as performing art for climbing as performance art. The former is the way the ascent is portrayed in words, photographs, or film. The latter—what was seen, felt, thought and feared in the moment—is privy only to the performers themselves.

I often find myself wondering about how the way an ascent is communicated influences the audience’s perception of what actually happened. This can range from flying in a big-budget film crew, to more subtle cues, like how a photo was cropped for Instagram, or whether one was shared at all. These words themselves are guilty, although I try to segregate my act of climbing from my act of writing about it.

My reluctance to share much about the climb stems from a fear that this blade is sharp on both sides—that the audience’s media-driven perception can in turn influence the climber’s own perception of the experience. Much like how the behaviour of quantum particles changes when they’re observed, climbers too, change our behaviour. Our egos feed off validation. Our eye becomes drawn to the viewfinder or to the stopwatch. We feel the presence of the audience cut through the ridgetop wind. We hear their applause over the crash of séracs in the distance.

I watched The Alpinist on the big screen when it was first released. While I never met Marc-André Leclerc, it left me feeling that much more went unsaid—that the real movie of his life was seen through his eyes only. A movie no one can rewind.

But anything is possible in cinema. In his account of Infinite Patience, Marc-André describes being unable to take a photo of a beautiful sunrise because his camera batteries had failed—“the shadow of Mt. Robson extending forever into the horizon against a red sky.”

From my sleeping perch high on the Emperor Ridge, I awoke to the same scene. Waves of red and gold crashed against the east face of Whitehorn Mountain while Robson’s summit pyramid shadowed the valley thousands of feet below. Was this movie magic or something more? Feeling as if I was suddenly not alone, I pulled out my phone in disbelief and took that photo. We can’t rewind each other’s films, but sometimes life lets us watch them together.

Nonetheless, I’m saddened to be left alone with my experience. My words are a lousy companion and my photographs are only worth a thousand lousy words. All I know is that I watched my film on the summit of Mount Robson. Where are you watching yours?

#8258. Boost the Performance of Your Canister Stove Without Blowing it Up

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

I had just finished pitching my tent and inflating my sleeping pad on a recent trip, and I could not wait to tear open the packet of dried miso soup I’d packed. My fingers were chilled from fiddling with guylines, and I craved the feeling of a steaming cup cradled in my hands. I screwed my ultralight stove onto a fuel canister, squeezed some water from my filter bag into a pot, and lit up. And then I proceeded to wait for what felt like ages. The flame was low and weak. Had I packed a nearly empty canister? No. The feeble flame was a harbinger, much like the leaves littering the trail: Winter was coming.

Canister stoves, like the ones most backpackers use during the summer hiking season, perform poorly when the mercury drops. Cold temperatures lower the internal pressure of the canister, causing it to falter, sputter, or produce a smaller flame. Regular winter campers often solve this problem by packing liquid fuel stoves like the MSR Whisperlite, which perform well in below freezing temperatures. Some canister stoves have a built-in pressure regulator that helps them stay efficient in the cold. But not every backpacker wants to shell out for an entire quiver of camp stoves. That’s where a little innovation comes in: Keeping a canister warm, even when the ambient temperature is frigid, helps maintain pressure so you can boil water on a regular canister stove all year round. Do it the wrong way, however and you might end up scorching more than your food.

When it comes to boosting the efficiency of your canister stove in winter, the key is gentle warming. A fuel canister’s contents are pressurized; when it is cold out, your goal is to increase that pressure ever so slightly. But overheating—and thus overpressurizing—can cause the canister to explode.

Warnings printed on the side of a canister tell this tale. Most manufacturers caution users to keep a canister below 120°F. Heating a canister by rapid means, like placing it in boiling water is a very bad idea—just ask the guy who punched a hole in his ceiling trying to heat a canister for a fuel transfer.

How else can one warm a canister? One hiker on Reddit suggested sticking a chemical hand warmer next to the canister and enclosing it in an insulated pouch. But experts Backpacker spoke to did not recommend that method.

“You’re adding a continuous heat source while also insulating the canister, and there’s no particularly good way to monitor or control its temperature,” says Adam Wilcox, senior mechanical design engineer at Jetboil.

Hothands, manufacturer of popular chemical warmers, claims that their products reach an average of 135°F, and warns that the maximum temperature can surpass 158°F. Granted, this doesn’t mean that placing a hand warmer beside your fuel canister will immediately warm the fuel contents to that same temperature, but it does heighten your risk of dangerously increasing  the pressure. Gentle warming is a safer bet.

“Body heat before use or a controlled warm-water bath are much more predictable ways of warming a cold canister,” says Wilcox. “The key with water is warm, not hot, and avoiding excessive heating of the canister.”

For a quick boil, keeping the fuel canister inside your jacket for a few minutes prior to use may do the trick to increase internal pressure. Of course, the effects of this will diminish rather quickly as you run your stove and expose the canister to cold air. If you need to run your stove a little longer to cook a meal or melt snow, a warm water bath can provide safe, continuous warming. Place your fuel canister inside a dish or spare pot. (I like to carry a collapsible silicone bowl for this purpose.) Light your stove. As soon as the water begins to warm but before it boils, pour some into the dish surrounding your canister. You should immediately notice improved performance.

Shopping for a new stove? Springing for one with a pressure regulator can help it perform more consistently across seasons. MSR claims that its Pocket Rocket Deluxe can run at full power at a fuel canister pressure of as little as 16.5 PSI. (A full canister would typically be at 45 PSI at room temperature.)

#8257. New Research Shows Why Running Takes More Energy as We Get Older

Running can get harder as you age. Normal wear and tear takes a toll, and your body needs more energy to cover the same distance.

A new study, published in the Journal of Experimental Biology in November 2026, found that some muscles in older runners were weaker than those in younger runners. Other muscles overcompensated for those weaknesses.

“The aging process leads to decreased strength and volume of muscles, including the calf muscles involved in plantarflexion,” Changal T. Nguyen, MD, a sports medicine physiatrist, told Outside.

Dr. Nguyen is also a clinical assistant professor of orthopedic surgery at Stanford and was not involved in the study. “The calf muscles and Achilles tendon also become less stiff with age, so they work less effectively as a spring, she said.

The good news, Dr. Nguyen said, is that adding a few simple exercises to your routine can help keep your calves strong and your Achilles tendon functioning well as you age.

The authors of the new study recruited 18 runners with an average age of 26.1 years and 18 runners with an average age of 63.4 years. The study referred to each group as “young athletes” and “master athletes,” respectively.

The researchers measured the athletes’ Achilles tendon stiffness and plantar flexor movements. (The plantar flexor muscles—located in the feet, ankles, and calves—propel you forward and upward as you run.) Then, both groups completed two six-minute treadmill sessions at two different speeds—roughly 5.6 miles per hour (mph) and 6.7 mph.

They found that master athletes’ hips worked harder than those of younger athletes. Their ankles, on the other hand, did less work compared to those of younger athletes. Master athletes also exhibited weaker plantar flexors.

Some of these findings could be explained by decreased calf and Achilles stiffness, Dr. Nguyen said: “When the calf can no longer generate as much power at push-off, the body compensates by relying more on other muscles, such as those around the hip.”

The researchers found that master athletes also spent more energy running, and their energy cost increased with speed.

“One notable finding is that the gap in energy cost widened at the faster speed, from about five percent to about 13 percent,” Dr. Nguyen said. “This hints that the age-related deficit may grow as running demands increase, although the study tested only two moderate speeds, so whether the gap keeps widening at tempo or race pace is unknown.”

There are a couple of limitations worth noting. The study had a small sample size, and the runners were tested at only two speeds on a treadmill, Dr. Nguyen said. Because of these limitations, it’s uncertain whether the findings would hold in different settings—for instance, on a trail—or at different speeds.

Strengthening your calf muscles and improving Achilles tendon function promotes gait efficiency (the amount of energy needed to walk or run; a high gait efficiency means less energy is needed to complete the motions involved in walking or running), which can help you keep running as you age, Dr. Nguyen said. She recommended three exercises that can help with this.

Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

#8256. Ben Zartman Splices Climbing Slings In His Garage. They’re the Best I’ve Ever Used.

Ben Zartman at work splicing slings in his garage. (Photo: Courtesy Ben Zartman)

When Ben Zartman learned to climb near Mexico City in the early 1990s, no one he knew could afford climbing gear.

“All of us were poor, and all the gear was imported and so expensive,” he says. “Most of the guys at the crag were sewing their own shoes or making their own cams.” Backpacks, harnesses, quickdraws—if they could sew it themselves, they did. At the time, Zartman was in high school. He didn’t have a job, but he did have a knack for making stuff. It never occurred to him that doing so might be sketchy until he arrived in Yosemite for the first time in 1995 and partners refused to climb on his rack. They were astonished he’d made his own gear. He was astonished that they’d bought theirs.

Later that year, when a government shutdown forced Zartman out of Joshua Tree, he hitchhiked to San Diego and bummed a ride to Baja with some sailors. Over the next few years, he split his time between big walls and boats, getting better at both kinds of rigging all the while. Then he got married, had three daughters, and spent five years sailing around the world on a boat he’d built himself. Eventually, he got work in a rigging shop in Rhode Island. He spliced custom slings for workaday sailors, then for open-ocean racing boats.

“At one point, I was sitting in the shop, splicing these high-end Dyneema loops, and I thought, man, if I had these in Yosemite, I would have been the coolest kid at the lodge cafeteria,” he says. And he likely would have: the spliced, covered loops used in sailing are seamless: no bar tacks or stitching. Instead, one end of the loop is woven into the other like a snake eating its tail. When you pull, the ends suction against each other (Zartman compares it to a finger-trap toy), making the loop stronger under load than bartacked Dyneema.

“The idea fomented for a while in my mind, and in 2021 I started reaching out to every climbing gear manufacturer I could think of,” Zartman says. Letters and samples went out to Black Diamond, Metolius, Sterling, and others, asking them if they’d be interested in partnering on a product. Hardly anyone responded.

So Zartman did what he’d always done: he took the DIY approach. In 2023, he launched his company, Zartman Rigging. He joined the UIAA, mailed in slings for lab testing, and registered for UIAA labels. Once his gear was certified, the renowned gear shop IME, in North Conway, New Hampshire, started selling it. Rock and Snow in New Paltz, New York, and IME in Salt Lake City, Utah, were next. As his following grew, so did his offerings: a featherlight personal anchor system, seamless rappel back-ups, a rope-carabiner alternative called the Dreamlink, and a tiny rappel plate designed for 6-mm cord. The ideas come from Zartman’s experience climbing Yosemite walls; the materials come from his time on boats.

“The research and development budget in the [sailboat] racing scene is so big,” he says. “It’s a great place to take technology from. I’m at that edge—I make ropes for the fanciest racing boats in the world, so I’m able to bring that into the climbing world pretty quickly.”

The results are wild. The Dreamlink has a breaking strength of 43 kN (or, rather, he tested it up to 42 kN in a UIAA lab, and that’s when it broke their machine). The seamless runners are tagged 24 kN but break at 27kN. A fancy UV coating makes them essentially sun-proof. They don’t expire like other soft goods; you only have to retire them if the core becomes exposed. I have a double-length seamless runner that I use for building anchors and extending rappels. No bartack means easy setup, it racks well, and it’s pretty light. (Most traditionally manufactured Dyneema slings are tagged at 22kN. Mammut’s 120-centimeter Contact Sling weighs 28 grams, while Zartman’s version is 32 grams, the same as Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord.)

Zartman has a strong social media fan club, but he has plenty of critics too. Mountain Project commenters, he said, can be particularly vicious. Many scoff at the idea of a soft shackle or a seamless runner as gimmicky or unsafe. He’s not too bothered.

“Ray Jardine got scolded by all the Valley locals when he showed up with Friends,” he says, citing the first-ever cams. When other companies started making camming devices in the ‘80s, Jardine’s critics were forced to bite their tongues. Zartman is seeing a similar arc with his own gear. Several other climbing brands have started marketing soft shackles similar to Zartman’s Dreamlink. And in 2025, Black Diamond released its Infinity Cord, a Dyneema sling that uses the same bartack-free construction as Zartman’s and the same covered-loop splicing technique that sailors have used for decades. Black Diamond called it a “breakthrough in the evolution of cordelette engineering.”

Zartman says he’s unaffected by the new competition. “If there are people copying the concept, that’s good because that means the concept is good,” he says. In the meantime, he’s keeping his head down, focused on fulfilling orders and prototyping his next batch of inventions.

Zartman Rigging is gaining recognition, albeit slowly. Zartman does no paid advertising; about 80 percent of his business comes from Instagram. His top-shelf pricing likely tempers growth as well. For context, a 120-centimeter Zartman Rigging sling is $63, versus $40 for Black Diamond’s Infinity Cord or $14 for a basic Dyneema Trango runner of the same length.

“Because I make everything out of the nicest materials and by hand, it’s the most expensive gear on the market. It’s a luxury brand,” he says. “Which is ironic given that I started in Mexico with my own homemade climbing shoes.”

Still, he produces enough to keep busy. Recently, he was able to hire one of his daughters part-time to help him splice, tag, and quality-test each product. He’s now a member of the UIAA safety commission, helping the organization design new testing protocols around skinny ropes and other novel forms of cord. He’s shipping to Alaska and Hawaii. People have started recognizing him in gear shops and at crags. Things are taking off—despite what Mountain Projectors may say.

“To a lot of people’s surprise,” he laughs, “I’ve sold a lot of gear.”

#8255. Mandatory Race Gear You’ll Actually Want to Use

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Many ultramarathons, including Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc (UTMB) require runners to carry certain gear. Cade Michael spent years as an unsponsored elite trail runner honing in his mandatory race kit with items that he both genuinely enjoys using and can be found affordably. He did this by taking advantage of sales, buying second-hand, and borrowing from friends. Here he shares his tips for building out your own race kit, including his favorite items in his pack.

Mandatory trail running race equipment is a lot like American health insurance: We all hate it. We’re all tempted to skimp on it. And we all inevitably need it when we’re least prepared. Required gear (or most of it, anyway) doesn’t have to be a waste of money or space. After spending yeas as an unsponsored runner curating my mandatory race gear, here’s my guide to getting gear that you’ll actually want to use more than once every 365 days, including my favorite items in my pack.

UTMB, among other races, often has extensive gear requirements and—whether you like to admit it or not—it’s usually for good reason. Weather and conditions can change rapidly in the mountains, and when you’re pushing your body to the extreme for hours (if not days) on end, as a general rule of thumb, it’s better to have it and not need it than to need it and not have it—particularly for race organizers’ liability insurance.

For example, while it may feel ridiculous for a 100K on the notoriously hot Western States 100 course in Auburn, California to make you carry a rain jacket and emergency blanket, the 2025 Canyons 100K  (on the same trails) saw snow at the start and highs around 40 degrees Fahrenheit. Packing three layers, two pairs of pants, and multiple pairs of gloves might seem like overkill for a day spent backcountry skiing in February, much less a running race in late August, but at the 2025 UTMB, ultrarunning’s most iconic race turned into a game of surviving the winter storm-like conditions.

I know all too well the allure of going light. But much like Admiral Ackbar’s epiphany at the Battle of Endor, it’s (usually) a trap. At the 2026 Twisted Fork Trail Festival in Park City, Utah, weather forecasts changed drastically in the 48 hours leading into race day, projecting relentless freezing rain. I chucked on a pair of gloves and arm sleeves and figured I’d warm up plenty as the race went on. As soon as we hit the first descent I lost feeling in my hands, feet, legs, cheeks, and plenty of other places I won’t call by name. My heart rate plummeted and I struggled for the entire remainder of the day. Eventual women’s champion, Rachel Drake, on the other hand, donned a warm base layer, long tights, gloves, and vest loaded with extras. Drake is an MD/PhD, mom, and professional runner for Nike ACG. Be more like Rachel, and less like me.

But you don’t have to hate the gear you’re going to buy one way or another to participate in these events.

Quality, packable gear can not only serve to save your race should conditions take a turn through the night in the Alps, but it can also save your run or, heaven forbid, life, if you’re spending any time out on the trails. While you could probably get away with using children’s XXS sized Walmart rain pants, your niece’s tiny pinky swim goggles, and Amazon’s finest two dollar headlamp, you can also use the mandatory equipment list of your next ultra as an excuse to get quality gear that won’t sit at the bottom of your junk drawer until next summer.

Here are my tips and tricks for getting good, lasting gear that’s a little easier on your bank account than the race entry fees and international travel.

Required kit, in most cases, isn’t going to be the product you wear holes through everyday. One is built to be versatile, lightweight, and packable while the other is made for a specific purpose and durability. Some pieces of equipment, like your rain coat for UTMB, are ones you want to stand up in the most brutal of conditions. Others, like a secondary headlamp, are areas you might be able to save some weight and cash.

Lightweight, packable gear is usually updated every year just like the rest of a brand’s product line and often goes on sale during off-season months or discount days (ahem, Black Friday or REI member days). A lot of years, the only update is the colorway, so just get the highlighter yellow and own it!

Better yet, buy gear second hand. Many of the products I’ll list below I grabbed from resale sites like Poshmark or Mercari for a fraction of the retail price

It may seem obvious, but always get your size. It might seem worth it to save a few grams and get a women’s XXS when you’re in the Chamonix Arc’teryx store panic-buying a rain jacket 24 hours before the gun goes off, but I promise you it’s not. Get the extra ounce and future you will be proud of the responsible decision to get something you’ll actually put on your body.

If you’re questioning whether a piece of gear will satisfy the requirements set by race organizers for your next ultra, err on the side of caution. Get the marginal gains wherever you can within reason, but I promise you trimming two centimeters off your bandaging or emergency blanket will not make Col du Grand Ferret any easier or quicker.

People in your run club and or training partners have probably raced an ultra and used this stuff before. If it’s not something you will need time and time again, it’s OK to borrow it; chances are, they won’t need it in the next week or two anyway. The more you share, the more you save.

Get familiar with your equipment. Try it in training, just like you would a pair of shoes or a nutrition product. Being able to mindlessly locate and use your gear will pay dividends when you have no mindfulness left late into an ultra. Brand-spanking-new isn’t always best.

If you’re between two rain jackets, just get the one with the extra zipper. The best gear is the gear you use. Ruth Croft and Tom Evans won a historically cold and wet UTMB in 2026. When they bundled up through the night, I’m certain they were rocking the clothes they trusted to get the job done, not the ones that came in a few grams under. You’re racing an ultra marathon through the mountains, not a 5K parkrun.

Please keep reading, my opinions are important. Seriously though, whether it’s one of our gear roundups (shameless plug) or your favorite YouTuber, people put dozens of pieces through countless miles so you don’t have to. Take a few extra minutes to read a few pros and cons before you pull the trigger.

A lot of thought and stress can go into mandatory equipment, but don’t let it take away from the race experience. At my first UTMB race, UTMB Whistler in Canada, the cold-weather gear policy was implemented two days before the race due to a snowstorm. I’d just come from racing in California and Spain in September, so I didn’t have a suitcase stocked with skimpy mandatory equipment. Luckily for me, I couldn’t afford to grab a bunch of last-second gear and just used what I had with me. Retrospectively, my pack was a little heavier and bulkier than it could have been had I been properly prepared, but I didn’t think about the weight once during the race. But boy, was I glad to have warm gloves and a beanie that fit.

Here’s a list of some of my favorite mandatory equipment I’ve amassed over a couple of years of racing in Chamonix as an unsponsored athlete.

This one is totally optional and, frankly, probably only applicable for a shorter ultra like MCC or OCC during UTMB week. The mini phone is a great tool to have if you’re only out for a handful of hours. So long as you ensure you get a SIM card that has roaming and data enabled for whatever country or region you will be running through, it can call, text, Whatsapp, and even Strava. UTMB requires you to have a smart phone capable of downloading and using the LiveTrail app, and this Google Play Store enabled pocket rocket is the smallest you can get while satisfying the requirements. It also takes pretty cool retro camcorder-style videos. For the longer races like CCC and UTMB, however, it’s probably your safest bet to just bring along your standard, daily driver smart phone. You have to keep your phone on at all times throughout the race, and the number of charging bricks you’d have to haul to keep this thing running through the night outsizes any weight savings it might provide.

Typically, flasks are flasks. Your running vest will usually come with a couple that fit. That being said, I usually hate running vests. One of the primary reasons is the way traditional flasks sit in the sleeves, bouncing around and uncomfortably rubbing against my collarbone. My pro tip here is to check out flasks with smaller lids like these Hydrapak pocket flasks. Theoretically, they’re made to fit flush with your running belt, but I’ve found they are less bulky and front heavy in a running vest, too. (As long as they fit in the sleeves.)

A sure bet to be on the required kit list for almost any ultra is a waterproof rain jacket. UTMB’s specifications are rather persnickety, with required minimum waterproof rating, breathability score, sealed seams, and an integrated hood. The On Ultra Jacket lives up to demands while remaining paper thin, uber light, and incredibly packable. It can end up feeling a little too trash-baggy and unbreathable to be your workhorse running jacket, but nevertheless it’s a great piece to be able to throw in your pack anytime you head up into the unpredictable weather of the alpine.

For headlamps, I always keep a couple of options hanging around for the varying amount of daylight in different races. For OCC, for example, I opt for the Petzl E+Lite. It’s so small and light it’s an almost imperceptible item to carry and it uses nickel-sized 2432 batteries, but, as you might expect, that means it is useless for anything more than an hour or so in a pinch.

For longer races where you will inevitably be running through hours of darkness, if not the entire night, this is not somewhere to skimp on weight. A popular option in this category is the Petzl Iko Core, which features an incredible 500 lumen bulb, outstanding shine time, and a replaceable battery that sits at the back of the crown for stability. If you’re running UTMB, don’t forget to pick up the mandatory red light filter for fragile wildlife areas.

The crown jewel of mandatory equipment is the running vest. It’s what will hold all of your other mandatory equipment. It’s what will be in direct contact with your body and can make or break the convenience and comfortability of your racing experience. But, most importantly, it’s what will show up in all your post-race photos and make you look either super nerdy or really cool—by which I mean slightly less nerdy. In all seriousness, choosing your hydration vest is critical—and critically personal. Salomon and Nathan offer popular options that have dominated the category dating back to the cradle of civilization. (Hammurabi allegedly kept his chisel in an ADVskin 5L.) But the market is flooding with alternatives as the sport continues to grow, so there is no shortage of options. The most important things to consider are fit and layout. For my preferences, which is for my vest to feel as least like a vest as possible, the Tantrums Crest 6 and Kiprun Pro Team 5L have been excellent. The pocket layouts have tons of nooks and crannies that scratch my obnoxious need for hyperorganization better than keeping foods from touching on my Thanksgiving plate. They have minimal bounce, soft fabric across the shoulder straps, and offer a rear tunnel pocket for an extra flask. Both the Tantrums and Kiprun also come in light colors, a touch that seems a blatant choice for any piece of athletic equipment but was, until recently, a white whale on the hydration vest market.

A good cap is indispensable and obviously extends beyond race day. It’s not that deep, just get one that feels and looks good. Ciele is a sure fire way to fit in at the coolest run club in town.

Waterproof pants can be a tricky one. They’re probably the thing you’ll use the least in everyday training (save for the tinfoil-esque emergency blanket), and they’re one of the most expensive pieces of kit on the list. Getting a pair that satisfies UTMB’s specifications and doesn’t necessitate a 25-liter pack to fit is going to be steep. On makes the Ultra Pant compliment to the aforementioned jacket, but I use these Rab Phantom Pants. I spend a lot of time outside. Unfortunately, a remarkable amount of the outdoors comes home with me.

For years, I accepted this as the price of admission. I swept. I vacuumed. I swept again. And then one of the dogs would come barreling through the door, and we’d start all over.

Which is why the best piece of outdoor gear I’ve bought this year has never actually been outside.

The Shark Navigator Robot Vacuum with Self-Emptying Base is currently on sale for $280, down from $450. It’s nearly identical to the model I’ve been using for the past six months, but with a larger self-emptying base that can hold up to 60 days of debris. With the holidays coming up, I think it might be one of the best gifts you could give someone who spends a lot of time outside, especially if they have dogs.

I spent three years wavering over buying one. Surely I could manage to clean my own floors? Did I really need to spend hundreds of dollars on something I could do myself?

For the past six months, my Shark has been dutifully making its rounds, picking up the dirt, debris, and dog hair that accumulate between adventures. It maps my house, works on carpet and hard floors, and returns to its dock to empty itself. I can schedule cleanings from my phone, so my floors get vacuumed while I’m outside doing something considerably more fun.

It’s not perfect. Occasionally it gets stuck, and once it even threw itself down the stairs. (I see you, adrenaline junkie!) But overall, it’s held up well to six months of living with two dogs and two humans who aren’t much better about tracking dirt inside.

The part I didn’t anticipate was how much joy I’d get from checking the collection bin.

I’m apparently so deeply into my mid-30s that one of the highlights of my day is seeing just how much dirt this little robot has collected.

And now it’s not? And I didn’t have to clean it?

This thing isn’t going to put away my ski boots or haul me up the skin track. But it does mean I can spend less time cleaning up after my adventures and more time having them. And if that isn’t a great gift for someone who’d rather be outside, I don’t know what is.

#8253. Colorado Trail and Continental Divide Trail ‘Extensively Damaged’ After Severe Flooding: Here’s What We Know

This article was updated on November 18, 2026, at 11:48 a.m. with additional information regarding the condition of the Colorado Trail section 28 and the Continental Divide Trail.

In just over a week, two massive flooding events hit southwestern Colorado, destroying homes, businesses, and infrastructure across numerous mountain towns. But property is not all that the floods affected. Parts of both the Continental Divide Trail (CDT) and the Colorado Trail (CT) suffered damage that locals and trail organizations are calling “extensive” and “severe”, and which could take a very long time to repair.

“Rebuilding these damaged sections will not be quick, easy, or cheap,” Paul Talley, executive director of the Colorado Trail Foundation (CTF), said in a November 5 update on the floods. “But we are committed to rebuilding.”

As many of these areas are still inaccessible, there is very little confirmed information on their current state. Videos circulating online show missing bridges at key river crossings, and reports from the USFS and other agencies indicate that trailheads are damaged, and “heavy debris” is blocking some sections. But there has yet to be a full, official report on damage to these trails.

Here is what we know so far based on official updates, local reports, and videos.

Junction Creek is the CT’s southernmost section. Its trailhead, just outside of Durango, is also the CT’s southern terminus. Junction Creek Trail crosses multiple footbridges over the creek along its 19-mile stretch. A video posted to Instagram shows the Junction Creek trailhead sign that many hikers use for their CT terminus photo now standing directly at the edge of a tall wash filled with flood debris.

“Junction Creek Trail #553 suffered a near-total loss in places where it parallels and crosses Junction Creek,” a USFS conditions report from November 13 reads. “Miles of trail as well as multiple bridges crossing Junction Creek were wiped out, replaced with massive piles of boulders, trees, and other flood debris.”

According to the report, both the lowest trail bridge at 2.6 miles from the trailhead and the Walls Gulch Trail Bridge at 14.6 miles were destroyed. One social media video shows the first footbridge washed away completely. The USFS posted its own video of the road to Junction Creek to Facebook, showing a “20-foot waterfall” over the edge of the destroyed road.

“There is no doubt that trails across the forest have suffered severe damage,” the San Juan National Forest wrote.

In an interview with The Gazette, Talley said, “The Colorado Trail Foundation has never experienced an event that damaged this much trail. This is the largest section of trail ever damaged in our 52 years.”

Authorities claim that recovery work will likely begin in spring and carry into summer 2027 due to weather. They discouraged hikers from even attempting to set out on the area’s trails.

“Record flooding across Southwest Colorado has left San Juan National Forest roads, trails, and other infrastructure inaccessible, severely damaged, and, in many cases, impassable,” a USDA Forest Service Facebook post reads. “Don’t become a statistic—rescue will not be readily available due to the current demand for search and rescue services.”

The CTF said that it will be working over the winter with USFS, local partners, and volunteers to determine timelines and project budgets for the restoration efforts.

“It will be months before we can better understand what the next steps need to be on the sections damaged by climate events this season,” wrote Talley in his November 5 update.

There is even less information regarding damage to the CDT, which also passes through the flood-affected areas of Southwestern Colorado.

The Continental Divide Trail Coalition (CDTC) posted on Facebook on October 23, warning hikers that flooding had made “travel to and from the CDT trailhead at Wolf Creek Pass impossible,” and that “hikers may need to make alternate plans to avoid the area.”

On November 2, the CDTC posted another update for CDT travelers. “The extent of damage to the CDT, access roads, and CDT communities is still unknown,” it said. While the interactive map on its website shows no current closures of the trail due to flooding, the CDTC advised hikers to use “extreme caution and check with local authorities before visiting.”

Outside of Colorado, New Mexico also experienced severe flooding. However, Audra Labert with the CDTC told Backpacker, “The area of New Mexico near the southern terminus did not experience significant damage from flooding.”

While the full extent of the damage to these trails remains to be seen, what’s certain is that the CTF, CDTC, USFS, and other state agencies have a great deal of restoration work to do next summer. Volunteers will be in high demand, and Talley, of the CTF, promised to be open about how hikers can help.

“While we do not yet know what it will take to rebuild, we do know what we will need,” Talley wrote. “We will need our supporters, we will need our dedicated volunteers, and we will need that community spirit that makes the CT so special.”
